steps.title: Choose a contract check or a recovery path
steps.objective: Identify contract boundaries and distinguish programmer mistakes from expected operational errors.
steps.explanation:
A valid C++ argument can be semantically invalid: an int divisor may be zero. A precondition holds before an operation; an invariant remains true during the relevant execution; a postcondition holds afterward. Check parameters at the entrance. For recoverable errors, an early return (bouncer pattern) keeps detection and handling together with less nesting.

Assertions expose programmer mistakes; ordinary error handling handles expected bad input, missing resources, recovery, or orderly shutdown. Both may be useful: assert an internal inverse helper's nonzero argument, then retain a separate zero-case handler for release builds. Handling has development/runtime costs, but disabled assertions cannot replace it. An assertion can itself be wrong: a percentage range needs &&, not ||; review and test both boundaries.

Source: [LearnCpp 9.6, contracts, Asserts vs error handling, and limitations](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/assert-and-static_assert/).

questions.question: An internal division function requires a nonzero divisor, a loop maintains 0 <= used <= capacity, and a sort promises ordered output. Which classification fits in order?
questions.explanation: The divisor requirement precedes division, the capacity relationship is maintained during the loop, and sorted order describes the completed operation.

questions.question: Users may enter a zero divisor, but an internal helper assumes validation already happened. Which design preserves recovery in release builds and exposes broken internal calls during debugging?
options: Assert on user input and omit ordinary validation.
Use static_assert on the entered value.
Validate user input with ordinary control flow; assert the helper's precondition, with a separate error handler if graceful release failure is required.
questions.explanation: Bad user input is expected and needs persistent handling. A broken internal promise is a programming error; an assertion exposes it early, while a separate handler can remain when assertions are disabled.

steps.title: Enforce the falling-object contract
steps.objective: Implement an internal precondition before handling normal boundary cases.
steps.explanation:
assert from <cassert> is an accepted macro, not std::assert: true continues; false reports the expression/file/line (wording varies) and calls std::abort. It documents and enforces assumptions near their cause, where a debugger can inspect state, rather than hiding errors in output or losing that abort point via std::exit. Abort does not unwind normally or guarantee cleanup: do not rely on it to save files or close transactions.

Implement fallSeconds(height, gravity): assert gravity > 0.0 first, even for nonpositive height; then return 0.0 for height <= 0.0, otherwise sqrt(2 * height / gravity). Use condition && "message" for context: the literal converts to true, preserving the condition (|| would mask failure). Assertions can similarly flag unsupported paths, e.g. !relocated && "Relocation not implemented", but cannot implement the feature.

Build with C++20 and -UNDEBUG. The Linux driver isolates invalid calls, disables child core dumps, and requires SIGABRT. Adapted from [LearnCpp 9.6, Assertions and descriptive/unimplemented-case checks](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/assert-and-static_assert/).

steps.title: Make the counter independent of assertions
steps.objective: Move required mutation out of an assertion while retaining a pure contract check.
steps.explanation:
Runtime checks cost work, so release builds commonly define NDEBUG; debug builds commonly do not. Inspect project/compiler definitions rather than trusting the label: -DNDEBUG disables assert, -UNDEBUG enables it; option order matters. Locally, put #define NDEBUG or #undef NDEBUG before all includes, without a semicolon. Even #define NDEBUG 0 disables checks; a later source definition overrides an earlier command-line undefinition.

Repair recordVisit(visits): assert the starting domain 0 <= visits < 1000 without side effects, increment once outside assert, and return the new value. The starter hides ++visits in an argument that disappears with NDEBUG. Required assignments, reads, and other work must stay outside assertions. This internal contract is not arbitrary-input overflow handling.

Run both C++20 builds (-UNDEBUG and -DNDEBUG): valid-input behavior must match; debug additionally requires SIGABRT for -1 and 1000 in isolated, core-disabled children. New exercise for [LearnCpp 9.6, NDEBUG and assertion limitations](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/assert-and-static_assert/).

steps.title: Reject a broken assumption before running
steps.objective: Choose static_assert for constant-expression requirements and distinguish compile failure from runtime abort.
steps.explanation:
static_assert is a keyword needing no header. Its condition must be a constant expression; false rejects compilation with a diagnostic, not a runtime abort. It works at namespace or function scope, costs nothing at runtime, and remains active under NDEBUG. Messages are optional since C++17. Prefer it when the fact is available at compile time; ordinary runtime parameters do not qualify.

Type-size checks such as sizeof(int) >= 4 enforce platform assumptions; sizeof(long) == 8 restricts supported implementations rather than expressing a universal fact. Predict the failure below, then change slots to 8 and compile again. Source: [LearnCpp 9.6, static_assert](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/assert-and-static_assert/#static_assert).

questions.question: What happens when compiling this C++20 program?
options: It compiles and returns 0 because NDEBUG removes every assertion.
It compiles but aborts at the second static_assert during startup.
Compilation fails at the groups-of-four requirement; NDEBUG does not affect it.
questions.explanation: 6 % 4 is 2, so the constant condition is false. The message explains the rejected assumption without a runtime check.

questions.question: After changing slots to 8, could int checked(int value) { static_assert(value > 0); return value; } check ordinary runtime inputs?
options: No: value is a runtime parameter, so this static_assert condition is not a constant expression.
Yes: every assertion in a function waits until the call.
Yes, but only if <cassert> is included.
questions.explanation: The location inside a function is allowed, but its condition still must be a constant expression. Use a runtime assertion for an internal runtime precondition, or ordinary error handling for expected bad input.

steps.title: Apply both kinds of check to percentages
steps.objective: Complete the existing workspace's constexpr predicate and asserted internal helper.
steps.explanation:
Open the [workspace notes](workspaces/09/09_06/lesson.md) and [main.cpp](workspaces/09/09_06/main.cpp). Implement pure constexpr validPercent(percent), true exactly for [0, 100], and checkedPercent(percent), which asserts that precondition and returns the unchanged value, never a failure sentinel. The predicate must support static_assert and runtime calls. Predict 0/100 as valid, -1/101 as invalid, and checkedPercent(45) as 45.

Run the supplied Debug tests with assertions enabled; CMake also keeps them enabled. Invalid calls run in children requiring assertion abort. Keep the tests, add one meaningful case, explain why internal assertions cannot replace input validation, and submit with ./course check 9.6. This is the repository assignment, not a [LearnCpp exercise](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/assert-and-static_assert/).
